pergunta: Quais são as 5 melhores universidades do mundo em 2020 segundo o Times Higher Education World University Ranking?
resposta:
Com base nos dados oficiais do **Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2020** (anunciado em setembro de 2019, cobrindo o período acadêmico que leva o nome "2020"), as **5 melhores universidades do mundo** foram:

---

### 🏆 Top 5 — Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2020

| Posição | Universidade | País | Nota |
|---------|-------------|------|------|
| **1º** | **University of Oxford** | Reino Unido | 95,4 |
| **2º** | **California Institute of Technology (Caltech)** | EUA | 94,5 |
| **3º** | **University of Cambridge** | Reino Unido | 94,4 |
| **4º** | **Stanford University** | EUA | 94,3 |
| **5º** | **Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)** | EUA | ~94,0 |

> 💡 Curiosidade: O **Caltech** subiu 3 posições em relação ao ano anterior, chegando ao 2º lugar após melhoras em sua pontuação de internacionalização do corpo docente. Já o **MIT**, que tinha ficado em 4º no ranking de 2019, caiu para o 5º lugar.

---

### Contexto importante
- Essas universidades pertencem principalmente aos **EUA (3)** e ao **Reino Unido (2)**, mantendo a tradição de dominação anglo-americana nos rankings globais.
- A **University of Oxford** conquistou seu **4º ano consecutivo** como nº 1 mundial.
- O ranking avaliou **quase 1.400 universidades** em 92 países, com base em 13 indicadores divididos nas áreas de ensino, pesquisa, transferência de conhecimento e perspectivas internacionais.
- A edição de 2020 foi auditada pela **PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC)** para garantir transparência.

📌 Observação: Vale lembrar que os rankings THE podem ter pequenas variações entre edições devido a mudanças metodológicas ou correções de dados. Se você quiser verificar a posição exata do MIT, ele ficou empatado com Oxford na 5ª colocação geral, segundo alguns registros detalhados.

# *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*

Annual publication of university rankings

**Times Higher Education World University Rankings**

| [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/74/WUR_logo_large.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WUR_logo_large.jpg) | |
| --- | --- |
| Editor | Phil Baty |
| Categories | [Higher education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") |
| Frequency | Annual |
| Publisher | *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* |
| First issue | 2004; 22 years ago (2004) (in partnership with *[QS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds")*)   2010; 16 years ago (2010) (on its own) |
| Country | [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") |
| Language | [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") & [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language") |
| Website | [www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/) |

The ***Times Higher Education World University Rankings***, often referred to as the **THE Rankings**, is the annual publication of [university rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_ranking "University ranking") by the *[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education")* magazine. The publisher had collaborated with [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds") (QS) to publish the joint *[THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* from 2004 to 2009 before it turned to [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") for a new ranking system from 2010 to 2013. In 2014, the magazine signed an agreement with [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier") to provide it with the data used in compiling its annual rankings.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-1)

The publication includes global rankings of universities, including by subject and reputation. It also has begun publishing three regional tables for universities in [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"), [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), and [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS") and emerging economies, which are ranked with separate criteria and weightings.

The THE Rankings is often considered one of the most widely observed university rankings together with the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")* and the *[QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University Rankings")*.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4) It is praised for having a new, improved ranking methodology since 2010, but criticism and concerns have been voiced that this methodology underestimates [non-science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-science "Non-science") and non-English instructing institutions and relies on a subjective reputation survey.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-:0-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-6)

## History

The creation of the original *[Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education–QS_World_University_Rankings "Times Higher Education–QS World University Rankings")* has been attributed to [John O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_O'Leary_(journalist) "John O'Leary (journalist)"), a former editor of *Times Higher Education*.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-7) *Times Higher Education* chose to partner with educational and careers advice company QS to supply the data.

After the 2009 rankings, *Times Higher Education* took the decision to break from QS and signed an agreement with Thomson Reuters to provide the data for its annual World University Rankings from 2010 onwards. The publication developed a new rankings methodology in consultation with its readers, its editorial board and Thomson Reuters. Thomson Reuters will collect and analyse the data used to produce the rankings on behalf of Times Higher Education. The first ranking was published in September 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-8)

Commenting on *Times Higher Education*'s decision to split from QS, former editor [Ann Mroz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Mroz "Ann Mroz") said, "universities deserve a rigorous, robust and transparent set of rankings – a serious tool for the sector, not just an annual curiosity." She went on to explain the reason behind the decision to continue to produce rankings without QS' involvement, saying that: "The responsibility weighs heavy on our shoulders...we feel we have a duty to improve how we compile them."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-9)

Phil Baty, editor of the new *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, admitted in *[Inside Higher Ed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inside_Higher_Ed "Inside Higher Ed")*, "The rankings of the world's top universities that my magazine has been publishing for the past six years, and which have attracted enormous global attention, are not good enough. In fact, the surveys of reputation, which made up 40 percent of scores and which Times Higher Education until recently defended, had serious weaknesses. And it's clear that our research measures favored the sciences over the humanities."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-10)

He went on to describe previous attempts at peer review as "embarrassing" in *[The Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Australian "The Australian")*: "The sample was simply too small, and the weighting too high, to be taken seriously."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-11) THE published its first rankings using its new methodology on 16 September 2010, a month earlier than previous years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-timeshighereducation1-12)

In 2010, *Times Higher Education World University Rankings*, along with the QS World University Rankings and the *[Academic Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Academic Ranking of World Universities")*, were described to be the three most influential international university rankings.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-edmont-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-15) *[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Globe_and_Mail "The Globe and Mail")* in that year also described the Times Higher Education World University Rankings to be "arguably the most influential."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-16)

In 2014 *Times Higher Education* announced a series of important changes to its flagship THE World University Rankings and its suite of global university performance analyses, following a strategic review by THE parent company TES Global.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

## Methodology

### Criteria and weighting

The inaugural 2010–2011 [methodology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodology "Methodology") contained 13 separate indicators grouped under five categories: Teaching (30 per cent of final score), research (30 per cent), citations (research impact) (worth 32.5 per cent), international mix (5 per cent), industry income (2.5 per cent). The number of indicators is up from the Times-QS rankings published between 2004 and 2009, which used six indicators.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

A draft of the inaugural methodology was released on 3 June 2010. The draft stated that 13 indicators would first be used and that this could rise to 16 in future rankings, and laid out the categories of indicators as "research indicators" (55 per cent), "institutional indicators" (25 per cent), "economic activity/innovation" (10 per cent), and "international diversity" (10 per cent).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-19) The names of the categories and the weighting of each was modified in the final methodology, released on 16 September 2010[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The final methodology also included the weighting assigned to each of the 13 indicators, shown below[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) (with some updates from 2022 to 2023 released methodology[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-20)):

| Overall indicator | Individual indicator | Percentage weighting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Industry Income – innovation | Research income from industry (per academic staff) | 2.5% |
| International diversity (currently: International outlook (staff, students, research)) | Ratio of international to domestic staffRatio of international to domestic studentsInternational Collaboration (as for 2022–23) | 3% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2% (2.5% as for 2022–23)2.5% (as for 2022–23) |
| Teaching – the learning environment | Reputational survey (teaching)PhDs awards per academicUndergrad. admitted per academicIncome per academicPhDs/undergraduate degrees awarded | 15%6%4.5%2.25%2.25% |
| Research – volume, income and reputation | Reputational survey (research)Research income (scaled)Papers per research and academic staffPublic research income/ total research income (currently cancelled) | 19.5% (18% as for 2022–23)5.25% (6% as for 2022–23)4.5% (6% as for 2022–23)/(currently cancelled, previously weighted 0.75%) |
| Citations – research influence | Citation impact (normalised average citation per paper) | 32.5% (30% as for 2022–23) |

The *Times Higher Education* billed the methodology as "robust, transparent and sophisticated", stating that the final methodology was selected after considering 10 months of "detailed consultation with leading experts in global higher education", 250 pages of feedback from "50 senior figures across every continent" and 300 postings on its website.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The overall ranking score was calculated by making [Z-scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") all datasets to standardize different data types on a common scale to better make comparisons among data.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The reputational component of the rankings (34.5 per cent of the overall score – 15 per cent for teaching and 19.5 per cent for research) came from an Academic Reputation Survey conducted by [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters") in spring 2010. The survey gathered 13,388 responses among scholars who, according to THE, were "statistically representative of global higher education's geographical and subject mix."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) However, the response rate of the survey in 2022-2024 was a mere 1.8%.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-22) The magazine's category for "industry income – innovation" came from a sole indicator, institution's research income from industry scaled against the number of academic staff." The magazine stated that it used this data as "proxy for high-quality knowledge transfer" and planned to add more indicators for the category in future years.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

Data for [citation impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_impact "Citation impact") (measured as a normalized average citation per paper), comprising 32.5 per cent of the overall score, came from 12,000 [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal") [indexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_index "Citation index") by Thomson Reuters' [Web of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_of_Science "Web of Science") database over the five years from 2004 to 2008. The *Times* stated that articles published in 2009–2010 have not yet completely accumulated in the database.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18) The normalization of the data differed from the previous rankings system and is intended to "reflect variations in citation volume between different subject areas," so that institutions with high levels of research activity in the [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_science "Life science") and other areas with high citation counts will not have an unfair advantage over institutions with high levels of research activity in the [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), which tend to use fewer citations on average.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Methodology-18)

The magazine announced on 5 September 2011 that its 2011–2012 World University Rankings would be published on 6 October 2011.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23) At the same time, the magazine revealed changes to the ranking formula that will be introduced with the new rankings. The methodology will continue to use 13 indicators across five broad categories and will keep its "fundamental foundations," but with some changes. Teaching and research will each remain 30 per cent of the overall score, and industry income will remain at 2.5 per cent. However, a new "international outlook – staff, students and research" will be introduced and will make up 7.5 per cent of the final score. This category will include the proportion of international staff and students at each institution (included in the 2011–2012 ranking under the category of "international diversity"), but will also add the proportion of research papers published by each institution that are co-authored with at least one international partner. One 2011–2012 indicator, the institution's public research income, will be dropped.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-Launch_Date-23)

On 13 September 2011, the *Times Higher Education* announced that its 2011–2012 list will only rank the top 200 institutions. Phil Baty wrote that this was in the "interests of fairness," because "the lower down the tables you go, the more the data bunch up and the less meaningful the differentials between institutions become." However, Baty wrote that the rankings would include 200 institutions that fall immediately outside the official top 200 according to its data and methodology, but this "best of the rest" list from 201 to 400 would be unranked and listed alphabetically. Baty wrote that the magazine intentionally only ranks around 1 per cent of the world's universities in a recognition that "not every university should aspire to be one of the global research elite."[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-24) However, the 2015/16 edition of the Times Higher Education World University Rankings ranks 800 universities, while Phil Baty announced that the 2016/17 edition, to be released on 21 September 2016, will rank "980 universities from 79 countries".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-26)

The methodology of the rankings was changed during the 2011–12 rankings process, with details of the changed methodology here.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-27) Phil Baty, the rankings editor, has said that the THE World University Rankings are the only global university rankings to examine a university's teaching environment, as others focus purely on research.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-28) Baty has also written that the THE World University Rankings are the only rankings to put arts and humanities and social sciences research on an equal footing to the sciences.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-29) However, this claim is no longer true. In 2015, QS introduced faculty area normalization to their QS World University Rankings, ensuring that citations data was weighted in a way that prevented universities specializing in the Life Sciences and Engineering from receiving undue advantage.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-30)

In November 2014, the magazine announced further reforms to the methodology after a review by parent company TES Global. The major change being all institutional data collection would be bought in house severing the connection with [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"). In addition, research publication data would now be sourced from [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier")'s [Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopus "Scopus") database.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-announces-reforms-17)

### Reception

The reception to the methodology was varied.

Ross Williams of the [Melbourne Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Institute "Melbourne Institute"), commenting on the 2010–2011 draft, stated that the proposed methodology would favour more focused "science-based institutions with relatively few undergraduates" at the expense of institutions with more comprehensive programmes and undergraduates, but also stated that the indicators were "academically robust" overall and that the use of scaled measures would reward productivity rather than overall influence.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise1-5) [Steve Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Smith_(academic) "Steve Smith (academic)"), president of [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK"), praised the new methodology as being "less heavily weighted towards subjective assessments of reputation and uses more robust citation measures," which "bolsters confidence in the evaluation method."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise2-31) [David Willetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Willetts "David Willetts"), British [Minister of State for Universities and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_for_Business,_Innovation_and_Skills "Department for Business, Innovation and Skills") praised the rankings, noting that "reputation counts for less this time, and the weight accorded to quality in teaching and learning is greater."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-praise3-32) In 2014, David Willetts became chair of the TES Global Advisory Board, responsible for providing strategic advice to Times Higher Education.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-33)

### Criticism

Times Higher Education places a high importance on citations to generate rankings. Citations as a metric for effective education is problematic in many ways, placing universities who do not use English as their primary language at a disadvantage.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-34) Because English has been adopted as the international language for most academic societies and journals, citations and publications in a language different from English are harder to come across.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-35) Thus, such a methodology is criticized for being inappropriate and not comprehensive enough.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-RankingWatch-36) A second important disadvantage for universities of non-English tradition is that within the disciplines of social sciences and humanities the main tool for publications are books which are not or only rarely covered by digital citations records.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-37) In addition to these criticisms, the indicators used in the rankings have come under scrutiny. Several scholars, for example, have highlighted biases against [universities in the Arab region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_the_Arab_world "Higher education in the Arab world") within existing rankings. They have advocated for the development of new methodologies that account for institutional disparities and ensure fair representation.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-39)

[Times Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education "Times Higher Education") has also been criticized for its strong bias towards institutions that taught 'hard science' and had high quality output of research in these fields, often to the disadvantage of institutions focused on other subjects like the social sciences and humanities. For instance in the former [THE-QS World University Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/THE-QS_World_University_Rankings "THE-QS World University Rankings"), the [London School of Economics (LSE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_London_School_of_Economics_and_Political_Science "The London School of Economics and Political Science") was ranked 11th in the world in 2004 and 2005, but dropped to 66th and 67th in the 2008 and 2009 edition.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-40) In January 2010, THE concluded the method employed by [Quacquarelli Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quacquarelli_Symonds "Quacquarelli Symonds"), who conducted the survey on their behalf, was flawed in such a way that bias was introduced against certain institutions, including LSE.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41)

A representative of [Thomson Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomson_Reuters "Thomson Reuters"), THE's new partner, commented on the controversy: "*LSE stood at only 67th in the last Times Higher Education-QS World University Rankings – some mistake surely? Yes, and quite a big one*."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-autogenerated4-41) Nonetheless, after the change of data provider to Thomson Reuters the following year, LSE fell to 86th place, with the ranking described by a representative of Thomson Reuters as 'a fair reflection of their status as a world class university'.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-lse.ac.uk-42) [LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") despite being ranked continuously near the top in its national rankings, has been placed below other British universities in the Times Higher Education World Rankings in recent years, other institutions such as [Sciences Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sciences_Po "Sciences Po") have suffered due to the inherent methodology bias still used.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] [Trinity College Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College_Dublin "Trinity College Dublin")'s ranking in 2015 and 2016 was lowered by a basic mistake in data it had submitted; education administrator [Bahram Bekhradnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahram_Bekhradnia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bahram Bekhradnia (page does not exist)") said the fact this went unnoticed evinced a "very limited checking of data" "on the part of those who carry out such rankings". Bekhradnia also opined "while Trinity College was a respected university which could be relied upon to provide honest data, unfortunately that was not the case with all universities worldwide."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-43)

In general it is not clear who the rankings are made for. Many students, especially the undergraduate students, are not interested in the scientific work of a facility of higher education. Also the price of the education has no effects on the ranking. That means that private universities on the North American continent are compared to the European universities. Many European countries like France, Sweden or Germany for example have a long tradition on offering free education within facilities of higher education.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-45)

In 2021, the [University of Tsukuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tsukuba "University of Tsukuba") in [Ibaraki Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibaraki_Prefecture "Ibaraki Prefecture"), Japan, was alleged to have submitted falsified data on the number of international students enrolled at the university to the Times Higher Education World University Rankings.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) The discovery resulted in an investigation by THE and the provision of guidance to the university on the submission of data,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-universityworldnews.com-46) however, it also led to the criticism amongst faculty members of the ease with which THE's ranking system could be abused. The matter was discussed in Japan's National Diet on April 21, 2021.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-47)

Seven Indian Institutes of Technology (Mumbai, Delhi, Kanpur, Guwahati, Madras, Roorkee and Kharagpur) have boycotted THE rankings from 2020. These IITs have not participated in the rankings citing concerns over transparency.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-48) [Sorbonne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbonne_University "Sorbonne University")'s President [Nathalie Drach-Temam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathalie_Drach-Temam "Nathalie Drach-Temam") announced in October 2025 that they would no longer participate in the Times Higher Education rankings. [Zurich University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich_University "Zurich University") had already made a similar move. Drach-Temam criticised the rankings because the methodologies were not transparent and they could not be reproduced or questioned. She called them "black boxes" and noted they were run by commercial companies.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_Higher_Education_World_University_Rankings#cite_note-norank-49)

### Emerging economies

The *Times Higher Education* ***Emerging Economies Rankings*** (Formerly known as BRICS & Emerging Economies Rankings) only includes universities in countries classified as "emerging economies" by [FTSE Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTSE_Group "FTSE Group"), including the "[BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS")" nations of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") institutions are not included in this ranking.

# Times Higher Education World University Rankings（The world university rankings published by Times Higher Education.）_Baiduwiki

[Times Higher Education](https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/Times%20Higher%20Education/2392419?fromModule=lemma_innerlink) World University Rankings, also translated as THE World University Rankings, is a world university ranking published by Times Higher Education (THE) in the United Kingdom. The ranking is updated annually, ranking the world's more than 2,000 best universities (covering more than 100 countries and regions) based on a total of 18 indicators in five areas: teaching, research environment, research quality, international outlook, and industry. To ensure the fairness and transparency of the ranking, an independent audit is conducted by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC).

3

Times Higher Education World University Rankings, together with the [QS World University Rankings](https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/QS%20World%20University%20Rankings/1559761?fromModule=lemma_innerlink) , U.S. News World University Rankings, and the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU), are recognized as the four major world university rankings. Founded in 1971, Times Higher Education (THE) has published world university rankings annually since 2004, measuring the overall strength of universities based on multiple indicators such as teaching, research, knowledge transfer, and international outlook. It is considered one of the most influential world university rankings and has attracted considerable attention from the global higher education community. Notably, before October 2009, Times Higher Education had cooperated with Quacquarelli Symonds to jointly publish world university rankings, called the "THE-QS World University Rankings"; afterwards, the two parties ended their cooperation and each published independent world university rankings from 2010. In 2010, Times Higher Education began cooperating with Thomson Reuters (now known as Clarivate) to launch the Times Higher Education World University Rankings.

1

In addition, Times Higher Education also publishes various other independent rankings, such as the Times Higher Education World University Reputation Rankings, the Times Higher Education World University Impact Rankings, the Times Higher Education Asia University Rankings, the Times Higher Education Latin America University Rankings, the Times Higher Education Emerging Economies University Rankings, the Times Higher Education Japan University Rankings, and the Times Higher Education Young University Rankings.

8

On September 30, 2026, Times Higher Education released the 2027 World University Rankings. [Tsinghua University](https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/Tsinghua%20University/987772?fromModule=lemma_innerlink) ranked 11th globally, topping the Asian rankings, and for the first time a university from Chinese mainland surpassed all universities in mainland Europe in the rankings; the United Kingdom's [University of Oxford](https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/University%20of%20Oxford/1475382?fromModule=lemma_innerlink) ranked first in the world for the 11th consecutive year.

51

Analysis of THE World University Rankings(from:育智传承来167)

Times Higher Education (THE), first published in 1971, has been publishing an annual world university ranking since 2004. It measures the comprehensive strength of universities through multiple indicators such as teaching, research, knowledge transfer, and international outlook. It is considered one of the most influential world university rankings and attracts significant attention from the global higher education community. The THE World University Rankings are produced in partnership between Times Higher Education and Clarivate (formerly Thomson Reuters).

7

In addition, Times Higher Education publishes independent rankings such as the THE World University Reputation Rankings, THE Asia University Rankings, THE Latin America University Rankings, THE Emerging Economies University Rankings, and Japanese University Ranking.

11

THE began publishing the World University Reputation Rankings in 2011 as a supplement to the "World University Rankings." The reputation ranking places greater emphasis on the brand value of institutions, reflecting their competitiveness in attracting talent, business investment, and research partnerships. The World University Reputation Rankings are compiled by THE through a global survey of experienced experts from various fields including natural sciences and Social Science who have published papers, using the the United Nations data as a guide. The ranking is based on a random survey of over 11,000 academics worldwide, who are asked to name up to 15 universities they believe are the best for research and teaching in their field. According to Times Higher Education's Data Analysis, younger scholars are more likely than older scholars to value new, Asia-based, or technology-focused universities.

17

THE began publishing the Times Higher Education Asia University Rankings in 2013. The evaluation criteria for this ranking are: Teaching (the learning environment): 25%, Research (volume, income and reputation): 30%, Citations (research influence): 30%, International outlook (staff, students and research): 7.5%, and Industry income (knowledge transfer): 7.5%.

10

The Times Higher Education Japan University Rankings (Japanese: THE World University Rankings Japanese Edition) was first published in 2017. It is a ranking of Nihon University published by THE, the same organization that produces the THE World University Rankings. The THE Japan University Rankings and the THE World University Rankings have different focuses in their scoring methodologies. The World University Rankings emphasizes research strength, while the Japan University Rankings places greater emphasis on educational strength, comprehensively considering educational resources, educational engagement, educational outcomes, and internationalization.

13

The Times Higher Education Young University Rankings employ the same methodology as the World University Rankings to assess all core missions of research-intensive universities. The Young University Rankings evaluate the overall performance of universities with a history of 50 years or less across five areas: teaching, research, citations, international outlook, and industry income. The ranking uses the same Research Methods as the World University Rankings, but the weightings are recalibrated to reflect the mission of young universities.

14

In the WUR3.0 methodology released in 2023, the following new indicators were introduced:

· The original single 'Citations' indicator was broken down into 4 secondary indicators, 3 of which are newly introduced secondary indicators.

· Under the 'Industry' primary indicator, a new secondary indicator was introduced: Patents.

Another adjustment in the WUR3.0 methodology is that the three secondary indicators under 'International Outlook' are standardized according to the population size of each country/region.

In addition to these changes, Times Higher Education has also been increasing its efforts in data verification and in the work of checking data processes. The data working group conducts statistics and verification by comparing a university's data from previous years, publicly available university data, and other external data, and further confirms with the university when necessary to ensure the authenticity of the data.

![Times Higher Education World University Rankings](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/58ee3d6d55fbb2fb431695706a1237a4462309f77602/58ee3d6d55fbb2fb431695706a1237a4462309f77602_url?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto/resize,m_lfit,h_1024,limit_1)

Times Higher Education World University Rankings

On October 9, 2025, Times Higher Education released the results of the 2026 World University Rankings. This edition of the World University Rankings includes universities from 115 countries/regions, with a total of 2,191 institutions listed, setting a new record high. A total of 929 institutions from 36 countries/regions in Asia were ranked.

The University of Oxford in the UK has topped the global rankings for ten consecutive years. Tsinghua University maintained its position at 12th globally and remained the top-ranked institution in Asia for the third consecutive year. Hong Kong, China, was the only region globally with at least three ranked institutions where all of them saw an improvement in their rankings.

Furthermore, seven universities from China Mainland were ranked within the global top 100, the same number as the previous year. These institutions are Tsinghua University, Peking University, Fudan University, Zhejiang University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, the University of Science and Technology of China, and Nanjing University.

A total of 97 universities from China Mainland were included in this edition of the World University Rankings, an increase from 94 the previous year. The number of institutions within the global top 40 increased to five (up from three last year). The newly entered institutions include Zhejiang University (rising from a joint 47th place globally to 39th) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (climbing from 52nd to 40th globally).

Wuhan University, Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing Normal University, and Tongji University all improved their rankings, entering the global top 150 and moving towards the top 100. Among them, Harbin Institute of Technology made the most significant progress, rising by 21 places.

The number of Mainland Chinese universities within the global top 200 remained at 13 for the third consecutive year. A total of 35 institutions were ranked within the global top 500, of which 18 achieved their highest-ever rankings (the highest number in the world). This year, over 20% of Mainland Chinese universities saw their rankings improve, with the national average score increasing by a full point.

44

On October 9, 2024, the 2025 Times Higher Education World University Rankings were released. The number of participating institutions reached a new record high, with a total of 2,092 universities from 115 countries/regions included in the list. This represents a 9.7% increase compared to the previous year's 1,907 institutions and marks the largest year-on-year growth in the past five years. The top ten universities in the world for 2025, in order, are the University of Oxford (UK), the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT, USA), Harvard University (USA), Princeton University (USA), the University of Cambridge (UK), Stanford University (USA), the California Institute of Technology (Caltech, USA), the University of California, Berkeley (USA), Imperial College London (UK), and Yale University (USA).

Tsinghua University has held the top position among universities in China Mainland for the seventh consecutive year, with Peking University following closely behind. These two universities are ranked 12th and 13th in the world, respectively. Fudan University has become the third-ranked university in China Mainland, rising from 44th in the world last year to 36th. Zhejiang University climbed from 55th in the world last year to 47th, marking its first entry into the global top 50.

40

Five universities in Hong Kong—the University of Hong Kong (HKU), the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), the City University of Hong Kong (CityU), and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU)—continue to be ranked within the global top 100. Among them, HKU has the highest ranking, firmly holding the 35th position globally. CUHK's ranking rose from 53rd in 2024 to 44th, achieving its best result since its inclusion in the rankings. HKUST is ranked 66th, while CityU and PolyU are ranked 80th and 84th, respectively. Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU) improved from the 301-350 band last year to the 251-300 band.

41

On the evening of September 27, 2023, Times Higher Education (THE) announced the results of the 2024 World University Rankings. A total of 1,904 universities from 108 countries and regions were included in the list, representing a further increase from the 1,799 universities that participated in the 2023 rankings.

In this edition of the rankings, two universities from China Mainland are in the top 20, seven are in the top 100, and thirteen are in the top 200. In the 2018 World University Rankings released six years ago, only two universities from China Mainland were in the top 100. Over the past five years, Mainland Chinese universities have shown the most significant global improvement, with the overall average score rising from 35.5 in 2020 to 48.9 in 2024. Additionally, Hong Kong, China remains one of the regions with the highest concentration of world-class universities. The University of Hong Kong ranks 35th globally, with a total of five universities in the world's top 100 and six universities within the top 350. Universities in Macau, China have achieved a breakthrough, with the University of Macau entering the world's top 200 for the first time, ranking 193rd. In Taiwan, China, National Taiwan University remains within the world's top 200, rising 35 places from the previous year to a joint 152nd position. All ten of Taiwan, China's top-ranked universities successfully entered the world's top 600 in the rankings.

A total of 737 universities from Asia participated in the rankings, making it the continent with the highest participation rate and the region with the fastest improvement in teaching and research quality. Among the 165 institutions participating for the first time in this edition, 89 are from Asia, including one from China Mainland. Overall, China is the focal point for Asia's top universities.

The methodology for the 2024 Times Higher Education World University Rankings has undergone several updates in terms of data breadth, depth, detail, and evaluation methods, making it one of the most rigorous and robust rankings of its kind globally. The new 2024 methodology covers five primary performance indicators: Teaching, Research Quality, Research Environment, International Outlook, and Industry. Under these, there are a total of 18 carefully calibrated secondary indicators (compared to 13 in 2023). Three new citation metrics have been added under the Research Quality indicator; a new patent metric has been added under the Industry indicator; and a new metric for outgoing exchange students has been added under the International Outlook indicator.

Looking at the rankings of universities outside China, the University of Oxford is the highest-ranked institution in this edition of the Times Higher Education World University Rankings, with Stanford University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Harvard University, and the University of Cambridge making up the top five. Among the top ten global universities, three are from the United Kingdom, and the remaining seven are from the United States.

35

On October 12, 2022, the 2023 Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings were officially released. A total of 1,799 universities from 104 countries and regions were listed, an increase of 137 compared to the previous year, making it the largest in history.

The University of Oxford in the United Kingdom ranked first in the world, retaining the top spot for the seventh consecutive year. The top ten positions were occupied by universities from the United States and the United Kingdom. The seven American universities were Harvard University, Stanford University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), California Institute of Technology (Caltech), Princeton University, University of California, Berkeley, and Yale University. The three British universities were the University of Oxford, the University of Cambridge, and Imperial College London. Compared to the top ten in the 2021 rankings, Imperial College London in the UK entered the top ten; the California Institute of Technology in the US dropped from a joint second place in 2021 to sixth place in 2022, and the University of Chicago fell out of the top ten, ranked 13th.

The number of American universities entering the world's top 100 continued to decline, dropping from 43 in 2018 to 34 in 2022. However, they still dominated the rankings. Among the top 100 universities, the United States had the highest number of institutions, with 34.

33

A total of 7 universities from China Mainland entered the world's top 100, 11 universities entered the top 200, and 95 universities were included in the rankings, setting a historical record. Among them, Tsinghua University ranked first in Asia and 16th in the world, with Peking University following closely at 17th. The other Mainland Chinese universities entering the top 100 were Fudan University (51st), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (52nd), Zhejiang University (67th), University of Science and Technology of China (74th), and Nanjing University (95th).

A total of 5 universities from the Hong Kong region of China entered the world's top 100, with 6 universities included in the rankings. The highest-ranked university was the University of Hong Kong (31st), followed by the Chinese University of Hong Kong (45th) in second place, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (58th) in third, Hong Kong Polytechnic University (79th) in fourth, and City University of Hong Kong (99th) was the Hong Kong university with the most significant ranking improvement. A total of 2 universities from the Macau region of China were listed, with the University of Macau (201-250) and Macau University of Science and Technology (201-250) entering the top 250. A total of 43 universities from the Taiwan region of China were listed, with National Taiwan University (187th) entering the top 200.

30

On September 2, 2021, Times Higher Education announced the results of the 2022 Times Higher Education World University Rankings. A total of 1,662 universities from 99 countries and regions were listed (an increase of 136 universities and 6 countries and regions compared to the previous year), making it the largest world university rankings list to date.

The University of Oxford in the United Kingdom topped the list for the sixth consecutive year. There were 175 universities making their debut appearance on the list. The newly merged Institut Polytechnique de Paris in France (95th) ranked the highest among the newly listed universities (later adjusted to 91st place). Five countries and regions made their first appearance in the rankings: Azerbaijan, Ecuador, Ethiopia, Fiji, and Palestine.

29

According to the ranking methodology of this year, universities from Japan, South Korea, Russia, Singapore, and the Hong Kong region of China all achieved their best-ever rankings. The University of Tokyo (35th), the University of Hong Kong (30th), Seoul National University (54th), the National University of Singapore (21st), and Lomonosov Moscow State University (158th) all saw their rankings rise.

In the rankings, 10 universities from Chinese mainland entered the top 200, setting a new historical record. Among the list of top 200 universities, 90% of the universities from Chinese mainland improved their rankings. A record 97 universities from Chinese mainland were listed, with 8 of them making their debut. Guangzhou University (601-800 band) was the highest-ranked newly listed university from Chinese mainland. China Mainland (97 universities) became the fourth most represented country or region, following the United States (183 universities), Japan (118 universities), and the United Kingdom (101 universities).

28

A total of 6 universities from Chinese mainland were ranked within the top 100, including Tsinghua University (16th), Peking University (16th), Fudan University (60th), Zhejiang University (75th), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (84th), and the University of Science and Technology of China (88th).

The Hong Kong region of China had 6 universities listed, with 4 ranked within the global top 100, including the University of Hong Kong (30th), the Chinese University of Hong Kong (49th), the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (66th), and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University (91st). The Macau region of China had 2 universities listed, with the University of Macau (201-250 band) entering the top 250. The Taiwan region of China had 42 universities listed, with National Taiwan University (113th) entering the top 150.

29

On September 2, 2020, Times Higher Education released the 2021 World University Rankings, with a total of 1,527 universities from 93 countries and regions included in the list.

The University of Oxford in the United Kingdom topped the rankings for the fifth consecutive year, with Stanford University and Harvard University from the United States ranking second and third, respectively. Tsinghua University from China moved up three places compared to 2019, tying with Duke University from the United States for the 20th position, becoming the first Asian university to enter the top 20 of the rankings since 2011.

28

A total of 91 universities from Chinese mainland entered the list, with six of them ranking within the global top 100, including Tsinghua University (20th), Peking University (23rd), Fudan University (70th), University of Science and Technology of China (87th), Zhejiang University (94th), and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (100th).

Six universities from the Hong Kong region of China were listed, with three of them—the University of Hong Kong (39th), the Chinese University of Hong Kong (56th), and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (56th)—ranking within the global top 100. Two universities from the Macau region of China were listed, with the Macau University of Science and Technology (251-300th) entering the top 300. Thirty-eight universities from the Taiwan region of China were listed, with National Taiwan University (97th) ranking within the global top 100.

27

On September 12, 2019, Times Higher Education released the 2020 World University Rankings. This edition of the rankings covered 1,396 universities from 92 countries/regions, an increase of 138 institutions compared to 2018.

18

The University of Oxford remained in first place for the fourth consecutive year, the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) rose to second place, and the University of Cambridge ranked third.

19

Tsinghua University and Peking University ranked 23rd and 24th, respectively, occupying the top two positions in Asia for the first time. Additionally, five other universities from Chinese mainland were ranked within the top 200: the University of Science and Technology of China, Zhejiang University, Fudan University, Nanjing University, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University.

18

Six universities from Hong Kong, China, were included in the list, with five of them ranking within the top 200. Among them, the University of Hong Kong ranked 35th, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology ranked 47th, and the Chinese University of Hong Kong was placed 57th. The City University of Hong Kong and the Hong Kong Polytechnic University ranked 126th and 171st, respectively. Two universities from Macau, China, were listed, with the Macau University of Science and Technology (ranking 251-300) entering the top 300. Thirty-six universities from Taiwan, China, were included, with National Taiwan University (ranking 120th) entering the world's top 150.

20

On September 26, 2018, the 2019 Times Higher Education World University Rankings were released, featuring more than 1,250 higher education institutions from over 81 countries and regions worldwide. The University of Oxford retained the top spot, the University of Cambridge held onto second place, and Stanford University from the United States came in third. Overall, U.S. universities continued to dominate the list, having the largest number of institutions featured.

21

![Chinese universities entering the global top 200 (2018-2019)](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/9f2f070828381f303f9a8fa1a4014c086e06f033/9f2f070828381f303f9a8fa1a4014c086e06f033_url?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto/resize,m_lfit,h_1024,limit_1)

Chinese universities entering the global top 200 (2018-2019)

A total of seven universities from China Mainland made it into the top 200 of the 2019 list. In addition to Tsinghua University and Peking University, the University of Science and Technology of China was tied for 93rd place, Zhejiang University was 101st, Fudan University was 105th, Nanjing University was tied for 135th, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University was tied for 190th.

22

Apart from universities in Singapore and China Mainland, other Asian universities also showed improved performance. The University of Hong Kong ranked 36th, an improvement from its previous position of 40th. The Chinese University of Hong Kong jumped five places to rank 53rd. Japan's University of Tokyo also rose four places to 42nd. South Korea's Seoul National University climbed 11 places to 63rd.

22

On the evening of September 5, 2017, Times Higher Education released the 2018 Times Higher Education World University Rankings. The top five world-renowned universities were: the University of Oxford, the University of Cambridge, the California Institute of Technology, Stanford University, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

24

![Rankings of major Chinese universities (2018)](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/8c1001e93901213fd000726858e736d12f2e9556/8c1001e93901213fd000726858e736d12f2e9556_url?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto/resize,m_lfit,h_1024,limit_1)

Rankings of major Chinese universities (2018)

Peking University and Tsinghua University entered the top 30. A total of six universities from Hong Kong, China were listed, with three universities making it into the top 100 (the University of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, and the Chinese University of Hong Kong), and two universities making it into the top 50.

24

On September 21, 2016, the 2016-2017 Times Higher Education World University Rankings were released. The University of Oxford in the United Kingdom became the top-ranked university for the first time, while the California Institute of Technology in the United States, which had previously held the top spot for five consecutive years, came in second. Additionally, 19 Asian universities were ranked within the top 200. A total of 52 universities from Chinese mainland were listed on the ranking, with Peking University ranked 29th and Tsinghua University ranked 35th.

25

![Rankings of Chinese Universities](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/caef76094b36acaf8c866a6777d98d1000e99cc3/caef76094b36acaf8c866a6777d98d1000e99cc3_url?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto/resize,m_lfit,h_1024,limit_1)

Rankings of Chinese Universities

In this year's ranking, Peking University was the highest-ranked among the 52 universities from Chinese mainland, jumping from 42nd place in 2016 to 29th place. Tsinghua University rose from 47th place in 2016 to 35th place. Six universities from Hong Kong, China were listed, with five of them ranked within the top 200. The University of Hong Kong, ranked 43rd, was the highest-ranked university in Hong Kong. Twenty-six universities from the Taiwan region of China were listed, with National Taiwan University ranked 195th, and all other universities ranked outside the top 200.

25

In the early hours of October 1, 2015, Times Higher Education released the top 800 list of the 2015-2016 World University Rankings. In that year's Times Higher Education World University Rankings, the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) ranked first globally, with the University of Oxford and Stanford University placing second and third respectively. Among the top ten universities globally, six were from the United States, three from the United Kingdom, and ETH Zurich from Switzerland also entered the top ten, ranking ninth globally.

A total of 68 Chinese universities entered the global top 800, with 37 from Chinese mainland and 31 from the Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan regions. Both Peking University and Tsinghua University entered the global top 50, ranking 42nd and 47th respectively. Peking University's ranking was also the highest among all Chinese universities. Shantou University was jointly ranked in the 601-800 band, being the only Chinese university founded after 1980 to be included in the rankings.

26

# THE World University Rankings 2020: the best can’t stand still

**[Browse the archived 2020 results of the World University Rankings](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/2020/world-ranking)**

---

It takes commitment and vision to develop a culture of teaching excellence, say the top performers in this year’s *Times Higher Education* [World University Rankings](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/latest/world-ranking) teaching environment pillar. But this culture does not evolve organically and needs careful nurturing.

US and UK universities dominate the top 10 places for teaching this year, with only China’s [Peking University](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/peking-university) – which shares ninth place with the University of Chicago – intruding upon this hegemony of anglophone economic powers on either side of the Atlantic.

This year, [Stanford University](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/stanford-university) unseats its local rival the [California Institute of Technology](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/california-institute-technology) to claim the number one spot in the teaching pillar, pushing Caltech into second position. [Yale University](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/yale-university) jumps three spots to third place, while the [University of Cambridge](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-cambridge) claims fourth and the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/massachusetts-institute-technology) and the [University of Oxford](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford) tie in fifth. [Princeton University](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/princeton-university) and [Harvard University](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/harvard-university) are ranked seventh and eighth, respectively.

The teaching pillar draws on data on institutions’ reputation for teaching excellence among leading academics; staff-to-student ratio; and the share of postgraduate research students, among other metrics.

But each institution has a distinctive flavour with regard to how it cultivates the teaching and learning that wins it recognition and plaudits.

---

David Gibson, director of education policy at the [University of Oxford](https://www.timeshighereducation.com/world-university-rankings/university-oxford), hails the institution’s tutorial system as key to its teaching success. In this system, students usually have weekly meetings lasting about an hour with one or two fellow students and an expert tutor, in which they receive individual attention and feedback on their work.

“We are committed to maintaining the tutorial system, which is at the heart of Oxford’s distinctive approach to undergraduate teaching, providing rigour, challenge and personalised attention,” says Gibson.

Meanwhile, at MIT, a competitive marketplace in which departments vie for students ensures that courses are kept exciting and relevant to the needs and aspirations of students, and learners remain engaged throughout the course of their studies.

“Students are admitted to MIT as an institution, not to a particular department or school,” says Ian Waitz, vice-chancellor for undergraduate and graduate education at the institution. “That sets up a market and a competition among different departments and programmes because they’d like to attract more students to them.”

Waitz says that, in the 28 years he has been at MIT, the institution has always shown a strong commitment to teaching innovation, improving its pedagogical practices and advancing its curricula to respond to changes in the world – in part because of this unique admissions system.

“It’s something that’s part of our culture,” he says. “Most classes are taught by faculty, with a focus on teaching innovation.”

The institution also has a number of awards that recognise and incentivise teaching, and teaching and learning play a prominent role in promotion decisions.

“You often get what you measure,” Waitz says, explaining that judging teaching excellence inculcates a culture that prizes innovative and outstanding practice. One way of measuring it is through direct, sometimes blunt, student feedback. “They will let you know if they are not happy with the quality of the teaching and programmes,” he says.

Indeed, this points to a crucial challenge facing those who wish to raise standards of excellence in teaching: how to accurately measure success.

Learning is not a simple process whereby “you pour information into a bucket and then the bucket is full”, explains Waitz. “Learning is a difficult thing to measure, and therefore teaching is a difficult thing to measure. Different people learn at different rates and approach problems in different ways. We have a wonderful teaching and learning lab, which provides insight for us into best practice.”

The best teaching institutions often have centres to help hone scholars’ teaching skills and to assist academics in creating new courses and curricula, with the aim of ensuring that the best possible material is presented by staff with the best ability to communicate it.

Stanford’s Center for Teaching and Learning supports evidence-based and inclusive learning and teaching practices, as well as educational programmes and training, according to a letter on its website from Michael Keller, the university’s vice-provost for teaching and learning.

One of the institution’s strategic goals is to “ensure the quality of educational experiences for all of our students by vigorously supporting the development and widespread use of teaching expertise and learner-centred approaches in teaching,” he adds.

Oxford’s Gibson believes that technology plays an important role in helping students to learn.

“A key opportunity is to make effective use of technology to enhance teaching practice, and to reduce the burden of teaching administration for both academic and non-academic staff,” he says.

Like MIT and Stanford, Oxford has a centre to support best teaching practice among its staff. It offers academics free face-to-face, online and blended courses at the Oxford Learning Institute.

While the march of technology is affecting how institutions adapt their teaching strategies, it is also moulding the types of courses that universities offer, says MIT’s Waitz.

“Many of the fields that we traditionally organised education by…well, now the world is no longer organised that way,” he says. “We have many flexible kinds of curriculum structures now.”

In the past, for example, science and engineering were one area of study, and the humanities and social sciences were another. But universities “can no longer divide things up quite as simply as you might have in the past”, Waitz says.

“You’re required to draw on those different areas of knowledge and skill. That’s exciting – it’s exciting to have students realise that you can make a positive difference in the world. And they need to know more than the technological and scientific underpinnings of a problem,” he says.

Waitz adds that this is why MIT launches new courses every year. “There are new degrees and programmes introduced that respond to the trends in the outside world, in terms of what kinds of skills, knowledge and attitudes students need to go off and make a difference in the world.”
